COMMUNITY PROPERTY AGREEMENT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Taylor Morgan

COMMUNITY AND QUASI-COMMUNITY PROPERTY DECLARATION
I, Taylor Morgan, am the surviving spouse or registered domestic partner of Jordan Alex Lee, who died on March 5, 2026. The following property was community property or quasi-community property of Jordan Alex Lee and Taylor Morgan at the time of Jordan Alex Lee's death, within the meaning of California Family Code §§ 760 and 125, or is property that Jordan Alex Lee's will or the laws of intestate succession passed to Taylor Morgan outright: the residence at 500 Market St, San Francisco, CA 94105. A certified copy of Jordan Alex Lee's death certificate accompanies this declaration. This declaration references the passage-without-administration provisions of California Probate Code §§ 13500-13506 and the confirmation procedure of California Probate Code §§ 13650-13660 for informational purposes; it is a private record, not a court order, and does not by itself clear title to any property.

THE SURVIVING SPOUSE'S OWN ONE-HALF ALREADY BELONGS TO THEM
Under California Probate Code § 100, when a person who is married or in a registered domestic partnership dies, one-half of the community property already belongs to the surviving spouse or surviving registered domestic partner by operation of law, and the other one-half belongs to the decedent. Probate Code § 101 applies the same one-half/one-half division to quasi-community property, but only when the decedent was domiciled in California at death. Both statutes describe the surviving spouse's own one-half as already belonging to them, not as property the decedent's estate passes or transfers to them at death — for that half-interest, the surviving spouse is not a successor of the decedent, and confirming it is a matter of documenting an existing ownership interest rather than of receiving a bequest or inheritance.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) Upon the death of a person who is married or in a registered domestic partnership, one-half of the community property belongs to the surviving spouse and the other one-half belongs to the decedent. (b) Notwithstanding subdivision (a), spouses may agree in writing to divide their community property on the basis of a non pro rata division of the aggregate value of the community property or on the basis of a division of each individual item or asset of community property, or partly on each basis. Nothing in this subdivision shall be construed to require this written agreement in order to permit or recognize a non pro rata division of community property."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 100(a)-(b), California Probate Code, division of community property on death of a married person or registered domestic partner (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=100.)
  "(a) Upon the death of a person who is married or in a registered domestic partnership, and is domiciled in this state, one-half of the decedent's quasi-community property belongs to the surviving spouse and the other one-half belongs to the decedent. (b) Notwithstanding subdivision (a), spouses may agree in writing to divide their quasi-community property on the basis of a non pro rata division of the aggregate value of the quasi-community property, or on the basis of a division of each individual item or asset of quasi-community property, or partly on each basis. Nothing in this subdivision shall be construed to require this written agreement in order to permit or recognize a non pro rata division of quasi-community property."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 101(a)-(b), California Probate Code, division of quasi-community property on death of a married person or registered domestic partner domiciled in California (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=101.)
  Known gap: This is California's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides for a decedent domiciled in, or with property characterized under, California law — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific decedent's marital property or estate. Sections 100 and 101 are separately numbered Probate Code sections addressing community and quasi-community property respectively, not subsections of one section, so they are independent sources. This document is informational only; it does not itself confirm title to any property or resolve any probate matter.

PROPERTY PASSING TO THE SURVIVING SPOUSE NEEDS NO ADMINISTRATION
California Probate Code § 13500 provides that when a spouse or registered domestic partner dies intestate leaving property that passes to the surviving spouse under Probate Code § 6401, or dies testate and by will devises all or part of their property to the surviving spouse, that property passes to the survivor and no administration is necessary, subject to the surviving spouse's power to dispose of community or quasi-community real property and to the surviving spouse's liability for the decedent's debts (both described elsewhere in this document). Section 13500's own text is not limited to community or quasi-community property — by its terms it covers whatever property the will devises to the surviving spouse outright, separate property included. Where the decedent dies intestate rather than leaving a will, though, § 6401(a)-(b) confines the surviving spouse's intestate share of community and quasi-community property to the one-half that belonged to the decedent under §§ 100 and 101; a different share applies to the decedent's separate property depending on what other relatives survive.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Except as provided in this chapter, when a spouse dies intestate leaving property that passes to the surviving spouse under Section 6401, or dies testate and by his or her will devises all or a part of his or her property to the surviving spouse, the property passes to the survivor subject to the provisions of Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 13540) and Chapter 3 (commencing with Section 13550), and no administration is necessary."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 13500, California Probate Code, passage of property to a surviving spouse without administration (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=13500.)
  "(a) As to community property, the intestate share of the surviving spouse is the one-half of the community property that belongs to the decedent under Section 100. (b) As to quasi-community property, the intestate share of the surviving spouse is the one-half of the quasi-community property that belongs to the decedent under Section 101."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6401(a)-(b), California Probate Code, surviving spouse's intestate share of community and quasi-community property (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6401.)
  Known gap: This is California's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides for property passing to a surviving spouse or registered domestic partner under a will or by intestate succession — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific decedent's estate. Sections 13500 and 6401 are separately numbered, independently enacted Probate Code sections in different divisions of the code, not subsections of one section. This document is informational only; it does not itself confirm title to any property or resolve any probate matter.

WHAT DOESN'T PASS WITHOUT ADMINISTRATION
Probate Code § 13501 identifies property that remains subject to full administration despite § 13500's general no-administration rule: property passing under the decedent's will or by intestate succession to someone other than the surviving spouse; property the will disposes of in trust; and property in which the will limits the surviving spouse to a "qualified ownership" (for example, a devise conditioned on the spouse surviving the decedent by a stated period, once that period has expired). This means § 13500 reaches only the interest the will or the intestate succession rules give to the surviving spouse outright — not property left to other heirs or beneficiaries, and not property left in trust for the spouse's benefit rather than to the spouse directly.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Except as provided in Chapter 6 (commencing with Section 6600) of Division 6 and in Part 1 (commencing with Section 13000) of this division, the following property of the decedent is subject to administration under this code: (a) Property passing to someone other than the surviving spouse under the decedent's will or by intestate succession. (b) Property disposed of in trust under the decedent's will. (c) Property in which the decedent's will limits the surviving spouse to a qualified ownership. For the purposes of this subdivision, a devise to the surviving spouse that is conditioned on the spouse surviving the decedent by a specified period of time is not a "qualified ownership" interest if the specified period of time has expired."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 13501, California Probate Code, property remaining subject to administration despite Section 13500 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=13501.)
  Known gap: This is California's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific decedent's estate. This document is informational only; it does not itself confirm title to any property or resolve any probate matter.

THE SURVIVING SPOUSE'S ELECTION TO HAVE PROPERTY ADMINISTERED ANYWAY
Probate Code § 13502 lets the surviving spouse — or the surviving spouse's personal representative, guardian, or conservator — elect to have all or part of the community or quasi-community property, and the decedent's separate property, administered through the probate estate instead of relying on § 13500's automatic passage rule. The election can reach the decedent's one-half of the community and quasi-community property plus the decedent's separate property, the surviving spouse's own one-half of the community and quasi-community property, or both. It must be made in a writing specifically evidencing the election, filed in the decedent's probate proceeding within four months after letters issue (or later, if the court allows more time for good cause), and before an order is entered under Probate Code § 13656.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) Upon the election of the surviving spouse or the personal representative, guardian of the estate, or conservator of the estate of the surviving spouse, all or a portion of the following property may be administered under this code: (1) The one-half of the community property that belongs to the decedent under Section 100, the one-half of the quasi-community property that belongs to the decedent under Section 101, and the separate property of the decedent. (2) The one-half of the community property that belongs to the surviving spouse under Section 100 and the one-half of the quasi-community property that belongs to the surviving spouse under Section 101. (b) The election shall be made by a writing specifically evidencing the election filed in the proceedings for the administration of the estate of the deceased spouse within four months after the issuance of letters, or within any further time that the court may allow upon a showing of good cause, and before entry of an order under Section 13656."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 13502, California Probate Code, surviving spouse's election to have community/quasi-community and separate property administered (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=13502.)

This document is informational only; it does not itself confirm title to any property or resolve any probate matter.

THE SURVIVING SPOUSE'S POWER TO SELL COMMUNITY REAL PROPERTY AFTER 40 DAYS
Separately from the no-administration rule, Probate Code § 13540 gives the surviving spouse (or the surviving spouse's personal representative, guardian, or conservator) full power, beginning 40 days after the other spouse's death, to sell, convey, lease, mortgage, or otherwise dispose of community or quasi-community real property, with any resulting buyer's, lender's, or lessee's interest free of claims by the deceased spouse's estate, devisees, or creditors — the same as if the surviving spouse had owned the property as separate property all along. The surviving spouse may record an affidavit of the facts establishing this right before or together with the instrument that makes the disposition. This power does not affect or limit the surviving spouse's own liability for the decedent's debts.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) Except as provided in Section 13541, after 40 days from the death of a spouse, the surviving spouse or the personal representative, guardian of the estate, or conservator of the estate of the surviving spouse has full power to sell, convey, lease, mortgage, or otherwise deal with and dispose of the community or quasi-community real property, and the right, title, and interest of any grantee, purchaser, encumbrancer, or lessee shall be free of rights of the estate of the deceased spouse or of devisees or creditors of the deceased spouse to the same extent as if the property had been owned as the separate property of the surviving spouse. (b) The surviving spouse or the personal representative, guardian of the estate, or conservator of the estate of the surviving spouse may record, prior to or together with the instrument that makes a disposition of property under this section, an affidavit of the facts that establish the right of the surviving spouse to make the disposition. (c) Nothing in this section affects or limits the liability of the surviving spouse under Sections 13550 to 13553, inclusive, and Chapter 3.5 (commencing with Section 13560)."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 13540(a)-(c), California Probate Code, surviving spouse's power to dispose of community or quasi-community real property after 40 days (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=13540.)

THE SPOUSAL OR DOMESTIC PARTNER PROPERTY PETITION — A SEPARATE COURT PROCEDURE
Beyond the automatic passage rule, Probate Code §§ 13650-13660 create a separate, optional court procedure: a surviving spouse (or the surviving spouse's personal representative, guardian, or conservator) may petition the superior court in the county where the decedent's estate could be administered for an order that administration is unnecessary because the property passes to the surviving spouse, and/or for an order confirming the surviving spouse's ownership of property belonging to them under § 100 or § 101. This petition does not reach property the surviving spouse has separately elected, under § 13502, to have administered as part of the estate, and a guardian or conservator may file it without separate court authorization in the guardianship or conservatorship proceeding. Because it produces a recordable court order rather than a private declaration, this petition is the mechanism typically used to clear title to real property or resolve a dispute about how property should be characterized — something an unrecorded declaration like this document cannot do on its own. Attorney's fees for the petition are set by private agreement between attorney and client, not by court approval, unless the client and attorney dispute the fee or its meaning, in which case either may ask the court to resolve that dispute in the same proceeding.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) A surviving spouse or the personal representative, guardian of the estate, or conservator of the estate of the surviving spouse may file a petition in the superior court of the county in which the estate of the deceased spouse may be administered requesting an order that administration of all or part of the estate is not necessary for the reason that all or part of the estate is property passing to the surviving spouse. The petition may also request an order confirming the ownership of the surviving spouse of property belonging to the surviving spouse under Section 100 or 101. (b) To the extent of the election, this section does not apply to property that the petitioner has elected, as provided in Section 13502, to have administered under this code. (c) A guardian or conservator may file a petition under this section without authorization or approval of the court in which the guardianship or conservatorship proceeding is pending."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 13650(a)-(c), California Probate Code, petition for order confirming property passing or belonging to surviving spouse (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=13650.)
  "The attorney's fees for services performed in connection with the filing of a petition and obtaining of a court order under this chapter shall be determined by private agreement between the attorney and the client and are not subject to approval by the court."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 13660, California Probate Code, attorney's fees for a spousal or domestic partner property petition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=13660.)

Sections 13650 and 13660 are separately numbered sections within the same chapter, not subsections of one section. This document is informational only; it does not itself confirm title to any property, constitute this petition, or resolve any probate matter.

WHAT COUNTS AS COMMUNITY PROPERTY AND QUASI-COMMUNITY PROPERTY
Family Code § 760 defines community property, for property acquired during marriage, as all property, real or personal, wherever situated, acquired by a married person during the marriage while domiciled in California, unless a statute provides otherwise. Family Code § 125 defines quasi-community property as property acquired by either spouse while domiciled elsewhere that would have been community property had the acquiring spouse been domiciled in California at the time of acquisition, or property acquired in exchange for such property. In short: community property is generally marital or domestic-partnership property acquired while the couple lived in California; quasi-community property is property that would have been community property had the couple lived in California when it was acquired, typically because it was acquired while domiciled in another state or country. Separate property — owned before the marriage or partnership, or acquired during it by gift or inheritance — is neither, and is governed by different rules not addressed in this document.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Except as otherwise provided by statute, all property, real or personal, wherever situated, acquired by a married person during the marriage while domiciled in this state is community property."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 760, California Family Code, definition of community property (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=760.)
  ""Quasi-community property" means all real or personal property, wherever situated, acquired before or after the operative date of this code in any of the following ways: (a) By either spouse while domiciled elsewhere which would have been community property if the spouse who acquired the property had been domiciled in this state at the time of its acquisition. (b) In exchange for real or personal property, wherever situated, which would have been community property if the spouse who acquired the property so exchanged had been domiciled in this state at the time of its acquisition."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 125, California Family Code, definition of quasi-community property (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=125.)

THE SURVIVING SPOUSE REMAINS PERSONALLY LIABLE FOR THE DECEDENT'S DEBTS
Receiving or confirming property under this mechanism does not extinguish the decedent's debts. Probate Code § 13550 makes the surviving spouse personally liable, upon the other spouse's death, for the deceased spouse's debts chargeable against the property described in § 13551, to the extent § 13551 provides (subject to a short list of exceptions in §§ 11446, 13552, 13553, and 13554). Section 13551 caps that liability at the fair market value, less liens and encumbrances, measured at the date of death, of three categories of property: the surviving spouse's own one-half of the community and quasi-community property (to the extent it is not exempt from enforcement of a money judgment and not administered in the estate); the decedent's one-half of the community and quasi-community property that passes to the surviving spouse without administration; and the decedent's separate property that passes to the surviving spouse without administration. In other words, the surviving spouse's exposure for the decedent's debts is capped at the value of what passed to or already belonged to them through this mechanism — not their own separate assets held apart from it.

  "The liability imposed by Section 13550 shall not exceed the fair market value at the date of the decedent's death, less the amount of any liens and encumbrances, of the total of the following: (a) The portion of the one-half of the community and quasi-community property belonging to the surviving spouse under Sections 100 and 101 that is not exempt from enforcement of a money judgment and is not administered in the estate of the deceased spouse. (b) The portion of the one-half of the community and quasi-community property belonging to the decedent under Sections 100 and 101 that passes to the surviving spouse without administration under this part. (c) The separate property of the decedent that passes to the surviving spouse without administration under this part."

This document is informational only; it does not itself determine any specific debt, its amount, or any specific surviving spouse's liability for it.

HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE SMALL ESTATE AFFIDAVIT AND FROM FORMAL PROBATE
The small estate affidavit procedure of Probate Code §§ 13100-13106 is available only if the gross value of the decedent's real and personal property in California does not exceed a periodically-adjusted dollar ceiling ($166,250 as of the most recent adjustment reflected in the statute's text) and 40 days have passed since death. The no-administration rule for property passing to a surviving spouse or registered domestic partner under Probate Code § 13500 carries no comparable dollar ceiling in its own text; it turns on the couple's marital or registered-domestic-partnership status, on how the property was characterized (community, quasi-community, or property the decedent's will devises outright to the spouse), and on how the property passed (by will or by intestate succession) — not on the estate's total value. The two procedures also differ in scope: the small estate affidavit is available to any successor of the decedent for the decedent's personal property (and, in a separate affidavit form, certain real property), while § 13500 and the related sections described in this document are available only to a surviving spouse or registered domestic partner, for property passing to that survivor specifically. Both procedures avoid a full probate administration in the ordinary case, but under § 13502 the surviving spouse can still elect to bring the property into a formal probate administration, and a formal administration remains available or required for any property that does not qualify for either procedure.

expectedJSON.body: Probate Code § 13502 lets the surviving spouse — or the surviving spouse's personal representative, guardian, or conservator — elect to have all or part of the community or quasi-community property, and the decedent's separate property, administered through the probate estate instead of relying on § 13500's automatic passage rule. The election can reach the decedent's one-half of the community and quasi-community property plus the decedent's separate property, the surviving spouse's own one-half of the community and quasi-community property, or both. It must be made in a writing specifically evidencing the election, filed in the decedent's probate proceeding within four months after letters issue (or later, if the court allows more time for good cause), and before an order is entered under Probate Code § 13656.

(2) The one-half of the community property that belongs to the surviving spouse under Section 100 and the one-half of the quasi-community property that belongs to the surviving spouse under Section 101. (b) The election shall be made by a writing specifically evidencing the election filed in the proceedings for the administration of the estate of the deceased spouse within four months after the issuance of letters, or within any further time that the court may allow upon a showing of good cause, and before entry of an order under Section 13656.

expectedJSON.body: Beyond the automatic passage rule, Probate Code §§ 13650-13660 create a separate, optional court procedure: a surviving spouse (or the surviving spouse's personal representative, guardian, or conservator) may petition the superior court in the county where the decedent's estate could be administered for an order that administration is unnecessary because the property passes to the surviving spouse, and/or for an order confirming the surviving spouse's ownership of property belonging to them under § 100 or § 101. This petition does not reach property the surviving spouse has separately elected, under § 13502, to have administered as part of the estate, and a guardian or conservator may file it without separate court authorization in the guardianship or conservatorship proceeding. Because it produces a recordable court order rather than a private declaration, this petition is the mechanism typically used to clear title to real property or resolve a dispute about how property should be characterized — something an unrecorded declaration like this document cannot do on its own. Attorney's fees for the petition are set by private agreement between attorney and client, not by court approval, unless the client and attorney dispute the fee or its meaning, in which case either may ask the court to resolve that dispute in the same proceeding.

citations.cite: California Probate Code, petition for order confirming property passing or belonging to surviving spouse
citations.quote: (a) A surviving spouse or the personal representative, guardian of the estate, or conservator of the estate of the surviving spouse may file a petition in the superior court of the county in which the estate of the deceased spouse may be administered requesting an order that administration of all or part of the estate is not necessary for the reason that all or part of the estate is property passing to the surviving spouse. The petition may also request an order confirming the ownership of the surviving spouse of property belonging to the surviving spouse under Section 100 or 101. (b) To the extent of the election, this section does not apply to property that the petitioner has elected, as provided in Section 13502, to have administered under this code. (c) A guardian or conservator may file a petition under this section without authorization or approval of the court in which the guardianship or conservatorship proceeding is pending.

citations.quote: The attorney's fees for services performed in connection with the filing of a petition and obtaining of a court order under this chapter shall be determined by private agreement between the attorney and the client and are not subject to approval by the court.

expectedJSON.body: Family Code § 760 defines community property, for property acquired during marriage, as all property, real or personal, wherever situated, acquired by a married person during the marriage while domiciled in California, unless a statute provides otherwise. Family Code § 125 defines quasi-community property as property acquired by either spouse while domiciled elsewhere that would have been community property had the acquiring spouse been domiciled in California at the time of acquisition, or property acquired in exchange for such property. In short: community property is generally marital or domestic-partnership property acquired while the couple lived in California; quasi-community property is property that would have been community property had the couple lived in California when it was acquired, typically because it was acquired while domiciled in another state or country. Separate property — owned before the marriage or partnership, or acquired during it by gift or inheritance — is neither, and is governed by different rules not addressed in this document.

citations.cite: California Family Code, definition of community property
citations.quote: Except as otherwise provided by statute, all property, real or personal, wherever situated, acquired by a married person during the marriage while domiciled in this state is community property.

citations.cite: California Family Code, definition of quasi-community property
citations.quote: "Quasi-community property" means all real or personal property, wherever situated, acquired before or after the operative date of this code in any of the following ways: (a) By either spouse while domiciled elsewhere which would have been community property if the spouse who acquired the property had been domiciled in this state at the time of its acquisition. (b) In exchange for real or personal property, wherever situated, which would have been community property if the spouse who acquired the property so exchanged had been domiciled in this state at the time of its acquisition.

expectedJSON.body: Receiving or confirming property under this mechanism does not extinguish the decedent's debts. Probate Code § 13550 makes the surviving spouse personally liable, upon the other spouse's death, for the deceased spouse's debts chargeable against the property described in § 13551, to the extent § 13551 provides (subject to a short list of exceptions in §§ 11446, 13552, 13553, and 13554). Section 13551 caps that liability at the fair market value, less liens and encumbrances, measured at the date of death, of three categories of property: the surviving spouse's own one-half of the community and quasi-community property (to the extent it is not exempt from enforcement of a money judgment and not administered in the estate); the decedent's one-half of the community and quasi-community property that passes to the surviving spouse without administration; and the decedent's separate property that passes to the surviving spouse without administration. In other words, the surviving spouse's exposure for the decedent's debts is capped at the value of what passed to or already belonged to them through this mechanism — not their own separate assets held apart from it.

citations.cite: California Probate Code, surviving spouse's personal liability for the deceased spouse's debts
citations.quote: Except as provided in Sections 11446, 13552, 13553, and 13554, upon the death of a married person, the surviving spouse is personally liable for the debts of the deceased spouse chargeable against the property described in Section 13551 to the extent provided in Section 13551.

citations.cite: California Probate Code, cap on the surviving spouse's liability for the deceased spouse's debts
citations.quote: The liability imposed by Section 13550 shall not exceed the fair market value at the date of the decedent's death, less the amount of any liens and encumbrances, of the total of the following: (a) The portion of the one-half of the community and quasi-community property belonging to the surviving spouse under Sections 100 and 101 that is not exempt from enforcement of a money judgment and is not administered in the estate of the deceased spouse. (b) The portion of the one-half of the community and quasi-community property belonging to the decedent under Sections 100 and 101 that passes to the surviving spouse without administration under this part. (c) The separate property of the decedent that passes to the surviving spouse without administration under this part.

The no-administration rule for property passing to a surviving spouse or registered domestic partner under Probate Code § 13500 carries no comparable dollar ceiling in its own text; it turns on the couple's marital or registered-domestic-partnership status, on how the property was characterized (community, quasi-community, or property the decedent's will devises outright to the spouse), and on how the property passed (by will or by intestate succession) — not on the estate's total value. The two procedures also differ in scope: the small estate affidavit is available to any successor of the decedent for the decedent's personal property (and, in a separate affidavit form, certain real property), while § 13500 and the related sections described in this document are available only to a surviving spouse or registered domestic partner, for property passing to that survivor specifically. Both procedures avoid a full probate administration in the ordinary case, but under § 13502 the surviving spouse can still elect to bring the property into a formal probate administration, and a formal administration remains available or required for any property that does not qualify for either procedure.
